podcast.title: Pioneering Double-Sided Discs (1908)
podcast.body: Columbia Records was the first record company to introduce double-sided discs in 1908, a revolutionary development in the early recorded music industry. This innovation significantly increased the audio capacity of flat discs compared to earlier cylinders. "in 1908, Columbia Records became the first record company to offer double-sided discs. This was radical and revolutionary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Digital Debris Part 1: B-Sides and Bonus Tracks

podcast.title: Innovator of Double-Sided Discs (1910)
podcast.body: In 1910, Columbia introduced and demonstrated its "Double Disc Records," which featured music on both sides, offering two different selections for a price slightly above that of a single-sided record. These records were playable on various machines, including Columbia Graphophones and Victor Talking Machines, and were promoted as providing double value. "The purpose of this record is to demonstrate the Columbia Double Disc Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the Record Store

podcast.title: First Art Director Hire (1938)
podcast.body: In 1938, Columbia Records in New York made a groundbreaking move by hiring Alex Steinweiss, a 23-year-old graphic designer, as the music industry's first-ever art director. This pivotal decision initiated the concept of distinctive album cover artwork. "Alex Steinweiss was hired as the first-ever art director for Columbia Records in New York."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: Pioneer of Original Record Cover Artwork (1938)
podcast.body: Columbia Records was convinced by designer Alex Steinweiss in 1938 to introduce original graphic designs for record sleeves, starting with Rodgers and Hart's "Smash Song Hits." This innovation significantly boosted record sales and led other labels to adopt the practice. "He convinced the executives at Columbia Records that some fancy artwork would be good for sales."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Firsts

podcast.title: Pioneering Album Artwork (1938)
podcast.body: Columbia Records hired 22-year-old artist Alex Steinweiss in 1938 as their art director, initially for store displays and newspaper ads. Steinweiss, recognizing the durability of new cardboard record jackets and the need to protect LP records from acidic paper sleeves, convinced the label to print artwork directly on the jackets. In 1939, for a new Rogers and Hammerstein record, he photographed a marquee he temporarily altered at the Imperial Theatre. Despite initial reluctance from management over the additional $2,500 cost, the record was released with his artwork and saw sales 900% above expectations, marking the first-ever example of album cover artwork. "In 1938, Columbia Records had an idea. They hired a 22-year-old guy named Alex Steinweiss, an artist who was very good at poster art."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Digital Debris Part 2: Album Artwork

podcast.title: Introduction of 12-inch LP (June 1948)
podcast.body: Columbia Records revolutionized music packaging with the introduction of the 12-inch long-playing (LP) vinyl album in June 1948. This new format, with its larger 12x12 inch double-sided packaging, demanded more content, especially as LPs were initially targeted at "high-brow" genres like classical music, Broadway show tunes, movie soundtracks, and jazz. This led to the commissioning of essays and editorial content, often written by journalists, musicologists, artists, or label executives, to educate listeners. "When Columbia Records introduced the 12-inch long playing vinyl album in June 1948, the game began to change."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Digital Debris  Part 3: Liner Notes

podcast.title: Introduction of the LP Format (1948)
podcast.body: Columbia Records released the first 12-inch, 33 1/3 RPM LP album in 1948, which subsequently became the main recording format, replacing the 78 RPM record. The inaugural LP featured the Philharmonic Symphony Orchestra of New York performing Mendelssohn's Violin Concerto in E Minor. "when the 12 inch, 33 and a third album was released by Columbia Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Ongoing History Book of Firsts

podcast.title: Unveiling of the LP (June 18, 1948)
podcast.body: Columbia Records officially unveiled the 12-inch long-playing album at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel in Park Avenue, New York, on June 18, 1948. Forty members of the press witnessed a dramatic demonstration comparing an 8-foot stack of 78 RPM records to a 15-inch stack of LPs. Edward Wallerstein demonstrated a 4-minute 78 RPM classical recording, abruptly stopping, then played a 22.5-minute uninterrupted version on an LP, stunning reporters. "The big day came on June 18, 1948 at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel in Park Avenue, New York. Forty members of the press entered a room where they saw a big stack of 78 RPM records. It was more than 8 feet high. Next to it was another stack of flat, some things, but it was only 15 inches high. Edward Wallerstein stood up. You're here to witness the unveiling of a revolutionary new technology, he said."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Acquisition of Sun Artists (1957)
podcast.body: Columbia Records secured agreements with both Karl Perkins and Johnny Cash on November 1, 1957, for them to begin recording for Columbia once their contracts with Sun Records expired. This move saw Columbia gain significant talent who were disillusioned with Sun. "Patrons and Johnny Cash, both made an agreement with Columbia Records, on November 1, 1957, that when their current contracts with Sun expired, they'd start recording for the new label."

podcast.title: Aretha Franklin's Early Career
podcast.body: Columbia Records signed Aretha Franklin in 1960 when she was 18, aiming to mold her into a traditional pop vocal star similar to Ella Fitzgerald or Dinah Washington. However, their strategy, which largely ignored the R&B market, was largely unsuccessful, resulting in Franklin accumulating debt to the label by the time her contract expired in 1966. "By the time she signed to famed Pop Label Columbia Records at age 18, Aretha Franklin was already a bit of a sensation on the gospel circuit."

podcast.title: Development of the Micro-Groove Record (LP)
podcast.body: Columbia Records was responsible for developing the micro-groove record, also known as the Long-Playing record (LP), as a solution to the limitations of 78 RPM records. Led by president Edward Wallerstein and in-house engineer Dr. Peter Goldmark, Columbia refined polyvinyl chloride (Vinylite from Union Carbide) to create records with grooves cut closer together and a smoother surface, resulting in more music per side (20 minutes on a 12-inch disc) and less noise. "It fell to Columbia Records to come up with a solution, which is where we get back to this plastic polyvinyl chloride, which had been refined by Union Carbide of the 1930s under the name vinylite. Led by a guy named Edward Wallerstein, the president of Columbia, and at in-house engineer named Dr. Peter Goldmark, Columbia started working on what they called the micro-groove record."

podcast.body: Columbia's introduction of the LP led to a format war with RCA, who refused to license the technology. Columbia introduced the 12-inch 33 1/3 RPM long-playing (LP) album, designed to hold many songs per side, in contrast to RCA's 7-inch 45 RPM single format. "This is when we encountered the format war between Columbia's 12-inch 33- to 3rd RPM long-playing album that held lots of songs per side."

podcast.title: Pioneering Vinyl Records in Response to Shellac Crisis
podcast.body: In response to the 1940s shellac shortage caused by World War II, Columbia Records tasked its chief engineer, Dr. Peter Goldmark, with finding a substitute material for phonograph records. Goldmark's team developed a solution using polyvinyl chloride (vinyl), an artificial substance previously used for sewer pipes in the 1920s. Vinyl proved more durable and allowed grooves to be cut closer together, increasing music capacity fivefold compared to 78 RPM shellac discs, thus catalyzing the recorded music industry's transformation into a multi-billion-dollar business with the introduction of 12-inch 33 1/3 RPM LPs and 7-inch 45 RPM singles. "This is where Columbia records stepped in with their chief engineer, a guy by the name of Dr. Peter Goldmark."

podcast.title: Quadraphonic Record Development (1970s)
podcast.body: Columbia Records was a key player, alongside companies like Sony and EMI, in the effort to develop technologies for encoding four distinct audio channels onto a single vinyl record groove for quadraphonic sound. These companies, including Columbia, ultimately agreed upon the SQ system as a shared approach. "A lot of companies worked on this, including Sony, Columbia Records, and EMI. And they all agreed upon a system called SQ."

podcast.title: Special 7-inch Records for Highway High Phi
podcast.body: Columbia Records produced special 7-inch records specifically for Chrysler's Highway High Phi in-car turntable system, introduced in 1955. These unique records were designed to hold approximately 75 minutes of music per side. They required many grooves and a slow playback speed of 16 and 2/3 RPM, resulting in "awful" audio quality, and were exclusively available at Chrysler dealerships. `"It was called the Highway High Phi, and it played special 7-inch records made by Columbia records that could hold about 75 minutes of music per side."`

podcast.title: The Record Jacket Invention
podcast.body: Columbia Records worked on 12-inch long-playing vinyl album technology, which highlighted the problem of acidic paper sleeves damaging records. Alex Steinweiss designed a new cardboard sleeve, known as the "record jacket," which the Imperial Paper Box Company patented. This new jacket became a "palette for a new art form" suitable for printing artwork. "He designed a new sleeve made from cardboard and got a box company to develop some special equipment. The result was known as the record jacket."

podcast.title: Vinyl Production Prioritization
podcast.body: Columbia Records, facing high international demand for vinyl production, strategically delayed the release of Depeche Mode's "Where Is The Revolution" vinyl single. This decision was made to ensure that sufficient units of the *Spirit* album could be manufactured and released first, with the single's vinyl scheduled for April 28th after album production was secured. "Colombia con ánimo de asegurar que se iban a poder fabricar suficientes unidades del álbum Spirit ha tenido que demorar la producción del single Welles y Revolución en Vinilo un poco de tiempo para dar prioridad al álbum."
